---
title: "Analysing clades and traits in a metacommunity"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6)
```

This article goes through the two analyses of metacommunity phylogenetics in the package:
the node regression of Leibold et al. (2010) with their daphniids, and the phylogenetic
gradient analysis of Peres-Neto et al. (2012) with simulated data, which are the methods
checked in the article on validation.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)
```

## Which clades respond to the environment?

`daphniids` rebuilds the data of Leibold et al. (2010) from the public survey: presences of
13 species in lakes of the northeastern United States, nine predictors and six biogeographic
contrasts. `node_contrasts()` codes each node of the tree as a contrast between its two
clades. This tree has no branch lengths; with them, `branch_lengths = TRUE` gives the coding
of the supplement of the article.

```{r}
nodes <- node_contrasts(daphniids$tree)
dim(nodes)
```

`node_test()` regresses each contrast on the predictors. The default of 9999 permutations
suits the false discovery rate. We use 999 here to keep the page quick to build, with
nodes in parallel on two cores.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
out <- node_test(daphniids$comm, nodes, daphniids$env, daphniids$biogeography, n_perm = 999,
                 cores = 2)
out
```

The p-values answer different questions, so this choice comes first. `p_max` tests the
association between predictors and phylogeny, and it needs both permutations to reject. With
13 species, permutations of species have little power, so nothing passes it here. Permuting
sites alone tests whether a predictor matters for that contrast, whether or not that comes
from phylogeny. The figures below use sites, as this recovers most of the results of the
article, and should be read with that limit in mind.

`plot_node_test()` places the results on the tree, as in Figure 3 of the article.

```{r, fig.alt = "Phylogeny of daphniids with blue symbols for predictors and red symbols for biogeographic events at the nodes, labelled with the names of the variables."}
plot_node_test(out, daphniids$tree, test = "site")
```

A tree of this size reads best as a phylogram. For very large trees, `type = "fan"` draws the
same plot in less space.

`plot_node_heatmap()` gives the direction and size of each association, as in Table S1 of
the article.

```{r, fig.alt = "Table of nodes by variables coloured by the semipartial correlation, with significant values in bold."}
plot_node_heatmap(out, test = "site")
```

A positive value means that the second clade of the node, in the order of the tree, is
favoured where the predictor is high.

## How much of the phylogenetic structure is due to environment and space?

For this question we need a tree with branch lengths and sites with coordinates, so we
simulate them with the generator of Appendix C of Peres-Neto et al. (2012). In the first
scenario, two independent gradients act on species.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
tree <- ape::stree(32, "balanced")
tree$edge.length <- rep(1, nrow(tree$edge))
tree$tip.label <- paste0("sp", 1:32)
gradients <- logistic_gradients(1)
sim <- simulate_logistic(tree, gradients[c("x", "y")])
keep <- rowSums(sim$abundance) > 0
comm <- sim$abundance[keep, ]
comm <- comm[, colSums(comm) > 0]
x <- gradients$x[keep]
y <- gradients$y[keep]
```

`phylo_vector()` tests whether a gradient is related to the phylogeny and, if so, gives a
vector of species values for the next step. Here we ask this for each gradient.

```{r}
first <- phylo_vector(comm, tree, x, n_perm = 199)
second <- phylo_vector(comm, tree, y, n_perm = 199)
c(first$p_max, second$p_max)
```

`trait_partition()` then splits the variation of these vectors among sites. The vectors are
chosen to fit the gradients, so this step only makes sense after a significant global test.

```{r}
vectors <- cbind(first$pev_brown, second$pev_brown)
partition <- trait_partition(comm, vectors, x, y, n_perm = 199)
partition
round(partition$semipartial, 2)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Bars of the fractions explained by environment, by space and by both."}
plot_trait_partition(partition)
```

The test of each trait against each predictor is a different question, for which ter Braak
(2019) is the reference.

## References

Leibold, M. A., Economo, E. P., & Peres-Neto, P. (2010). Metacommunity phylogenetics:
separating the roles of environmental filters and historical biogeography. *Ecology
Letters*, 13, 1290--1299. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01523.x

Peres-Neto, P. R., Leibold, M. A., & Dray, S. (2012). Assessing the effects of spatial
contingency and environmental filtering on metacommunity phylogenetics. *Ecology*, 93,
S14--S30. https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0494.1

ter Braak, C. J. F. (2019). New robust weighted averaging- and model-based methods for
assessing trait-environment relationships. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 10,
1962--1971. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13278
